articles.title: IND vs NZ: 'Rahul Dravid batted us into submission' - Kyle Mills recalls India's 2009 triumph in Hamilton Test | Exclusive Interview
articles.summary: WELLINGTON: New Zealand has always remained a tricky frontier for India. It's been 17 years since India last won a Test match in New Zealand.
articles.body: WELLINGTON: New Zealand has always remained a tricky frontier for India. It's been 17 years since India last won a Test match in New Zealand. Even India's famous win at Seddon Park in Hamilton in 2009, which sealed a memorable series victory for the MS Dhoni-led side, came 33 years after the previous Test series win in New Zealand.Kyle Mills, part of the New Zealand squad for the Hamilton fixture, vividly, but not fondly, remembers the game as his last outing for the Black Caps in whites."I remember that Test very well. That Test match was the epitome of the Rahul Dravid ‘Wall’. He batted beautifully and really dug in, batting us into submission. That was actually my last Test match, so not fond memories," Mills recalled in an interview with TOI.The Kiwi seamer, who took a solitary wicket in the match, still remembers getting Team India head coach Gautam Gambhir out leg before wicket, but he had overstepped, which gave the southpaw an early reprieve. Mills feels it could have been a different story had they taken the early wicket, but it wasn't meant to be."I actually got Gambhir out LBW; well, it was out, it was absolutely dead out, but my front foot was over the line, and Simon Taufel was the umpire and called me for a no ball, and then I was gutted because it would have been great to get an early wicket, and then who knows how the game would have progressed," says Mills.Gambhir scored 72 and partnered solidly with Rahul Dravid, and the two set a solid platform for the Little Master Sachin Tendulkar to dominate from. Tendulkar scored a brilliant 160, and his 260-ball essay was enough to bat the hosts out of the game."Rahul Dravid was amazing in that Test match, so was Sachin Tendulkar. You kind of think about some of the players you had in that series... Zaheer Khan was playing; they're generational cricketing greats, (Virender) Sehwag played that Test, (VVS) Laxman was also there. India had a brilliant cricket team during that period and potentially played as well... just a brilliant cricket team," adds Mills.The fixture turned out to be a cruel ending for Mills in more ways than one, as he also conceded the winning runs off Gambhir's bat in the second innings when India stormed home without losing a wicket.The former India opener now returns to the familiar territory but with a different challenge, and without the bat in hand. For Mills, Gambhir remains the "tough competitor" unwilling to drop an inch."He's always a tough competitor on the field, without question. No jokes were going around at all because he was always business on the field, a tough cricketer. Post-cricket, he got into politics and became a leader. articles.title: Exclusive interview | 'Donkey work' awaits Bumrah & Co: Shane Bond, Kyle Mills on Wellington's wind challenge
articles.summary: WELLINGTON: India's first stop in the two-match Test series will be the Basin Reserve in 'Windy Welly'.
articles.body: WELLINGTON: India's first stop in the two-match Test series will be the Basin Reserve in 'Windy Welly'. The entire squad, except Mohammed Siraj, has been training in the city since November 12 and will have two more sessions before taking the field for the series opener. The Basin Reserve is a challenging venue for any visiting team because of its open surroundings and strong winds, which usually blow straight down from one end.In simpler terms, a fast bowler has to be prepared to run into the wind and put in the hard yards for extended periods during a Test match. Former New Zealand fast bowler Shane Bond says both Wellington and Christchurch are windy cities, but the strength of the wind makes the former a little more challenging. He expects someone to do the "donkey work" for an extended period when the action gets underway on November 19."Christchurch is a windy town too. The biggest thing probably, the difference between Christchurch and Wellington is when the wind blows, it's the strength of the wind and it generally blows straight down from one end. So someone's going to have to do some donkey work into it. I've seen in the past that even if you're a first-class bowler at home, having to bowl into the wind at Wellington can present some real problems. Particularly if you bowl downwind for your state team and then have to run into the wind at Wellington. It is a specialised role. It can be challenging if the wind's up there," Bond tells TOI in an exclusive chat.The 51-year-old, who was on broadcast duties during the limited-overs series and is now busy with his ILT20 commitments, says there are calm days too, but teams should expect at least a couple of days when they will have to contend with strong gusts. When India played a T20I here, players found it difficult to keep their gear in place, with caps, sunglasses and other equipment repeatedly flying away. Can players prepare for such conditions, even if they arrive early? Bond doesn't think so."It's usually not like that for five days. But over the course of a Test match, you'd be expecting a day or two where the wind's pretty strong. It's pretty tough to prepare for. Most of the guys now, international cricketers, have played all over the world in all sorts of different conditions," says Bond.The weather in New Zealand has been largely pleasant during the day and chilly in the evening. More of the same is expected in Wellington over the next week, but players need to be ready for a demanding workout as the "wind can be draining"."New Zealand's not a particularly hot country, but the wind can be draining. You end up getting short spells into the wind from one end. Your spinner often does a bulk of the donkey work. So your fast bowlers, especially your attacking ones, rotate from one end downwind. You're trying to find a couple of bowlers who do the bulk of that work into the wind if it's strong," adds Bond.November is not the usual time for the start of a Test series in New Zealand, and former fast bowler Kyle Mills says the country experiences stronger winds during the period leading up to Christmas. He feels for the bowler who will have to run into the wind at the Basin Reserve this week."What tends to happen here in New Zealand in the spring, before Christmas, are more windy periods. We get a lot of strong winds, and Wellington traditionally has a lot of strong winds anyway. There's going to be an unfortunate bowler who's going to be bowling into the wind. In Wellington, you can't dodge that at all. But I think with both pitches, you're still going to get good pace and carry through to the wicketkeeper. You will get a little bit of swing," says Mills.The likes of Jasprit Bumrah, Anshul Kamboj, Gurnoor Brar, Prasidh Krishna, Akash Deep and Mohammed Siraj have spent enough time in New Zealand to become accustomed to the conditions. But come November 19, a date that holds painful memories in the Indian cricket calendar, it will be about who comes out on top in the battle against the wind.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: What next for Rohit? NZ struggles, advancing age put veteran's place under scrutiny
articles.summary: The batting conditions in India's five-match ODI series against New Zealand, which ended on Sunday, were far from straightforward, especially under lights.
articles.body: The batting conditions in India's five-match ODI series against New Zealand, which ended on Sunday, were far from straightforward, especially under lights. The ball moved in the air and off the pitch, while the tennis-ball bounce gave pacers plenty to work with.Even so, Rohit Sharma's returns were stark: 0 off 6, 23 off 28, 0 off 1 and 7 off 13. Looking leaden-footed on seamer-friendly surfaces and far removed from the batter who has scored 12,150 runs in 296 ODIs at 48.60, with 35 centuries, 63 fifties and a world-record 264, the 39-year-old managed just 30 runs in four innings at 7.50.For a player who has dominated ODI cricket since moving to the top of the order in 2013, such a lean run is rare. This was his 26th overseas ODI series across nearly two decades, and only the third in which he averaged in single digits. On three occasions, he has averaged more than 100.The only time he fared worse across at least four innings was against Sri Lanka 14 years ago, a series he later described as the worst of his career. Rohit made just 13 runs in five matches, averaging 2.60. Rohit's dismissals in New Zealand exposed his struggles against the moving ball. He fell to Jamieson in Auckland and Wellington, edged Matt Henry at Mount Maunganui and picked out midwicket off Matthew Fisher in his final innings.With the 2027 ODI World Cup approaching, every failure will fuel the age debate. Rohit was 39 years and 199 days old in his last ODI and will be 40 years and 180 days old when India face Australia in their World Cup opener in Cape Town. Every lean series will inevitably raise questions about his place in the team.He will have opportunities to regain form in the home ODI series against Sri Lanka, beginning in Vi-zag on Dec 13, and Zimbabwe, starting in Kolkata on Jan 3, 2027. Howe-ver, India's batting-friendly pitches may not test his reflexes as seve-rely as New Zealand's conditions.Rohit's struggles have brought India's alternatives into focus, with young openers Yashasvi Jaiswal, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi and Abhishek Sharma waiting for opportunities. Jaiswal, in particular, has been unlucky, having scored 285 runs at 71.25, including two centuries, in just six ODIs but struggled to find a regular place behind Rohit and Shubman Gill.The debate is now unavoidable: should Rohit play the 2027 World Cup? And are India running out of time to prepare alternatives if his form does not improve?There is a cautionary precedent in MS Dhoni's final phase. The former India captain, an all-time white-ball great, found it increasingly difficult to force the pace during the 2019 World Cup in England, where India exited in the semifinals. Will Rohit's final lap follow a similar path, or can he rediscover his touch and sign off on his own terms?It is no secret that the selectors had initially looked beyond Rohit for the 2027 World Cup and indicated that Lord's could be his final appearance in India colours. However, the Mumbaikar convinced the BCCI hierarchy of his worth and his desire to continue until the global event.That raises another question: was former chief selector and India pacer Ajit Agarkar right to question Rohit's place in the ODI side, even as the BCCI backed the superstar's World Cup ambitions? The reported disagreement between the two only sharpened the issue.Much will now depend on how the new selection committee, headed by former left-arm spinner Pragyan Ojha, views Rohit's form and future. Ojha, a former India and Mumbai Indians teammate of Rohit, will face a difficult call if the batter's lean run continues. Selection meetings are also attended by Centre of Excellence chairperson and former India batter VVS Laxman.There is precedent for selectors making tough calls on established stars. During his tenure as chief selector from 2012 to 2016, former India batter Sandeep Patil oversaw the transition away from several greats, most notably Sachin Tendulkar.Patil, however, believes Rohit deserves time to regain form and has backed him to make the World Cup squad. "Rohit and Virat are the kind of players whose class is permanent. Form is temporary. Not scoring runs in a series can happen. What is more important is the 2027 ODI World Cup, not this ODI series in New Zealand. As a big fan of Rohit, I would love to see him in the World Cup, but the decision remains with the selectors and Rohit," Patil told TOI on Monday.He said there was still almost a year to go before the tournament, giving Rohit time to recover, provided he stayed fit and competitive.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Green tinge, nice bounce': Rachin Ravindra on what awaits India in Test series vs New Zealand
articles.summary: New Zealand all-rounder Rachin Ravindra expects the pitches to become better for batting as the upcoming Test series against India progresses.
articles.body: New Zealand all-rounder Rachin Ravindra expects the pitches to become better for batting as the upcoming Test series against India progresses.While New Zealand pitches often have grass and a green tinge that help fast bowlers, Ravindra believes batters can score big runs once they settle down and play according to their plans.Ravindra also expects a good contest between the bat and ball in the first Test, which begins on Thursday at the Basin Reserve in Wellington.Ravindra explains New Zealand pitch conditionsThe 26-year-old said the green look of New Zealand pitches often creates questions about how the ball will behave, but he believes it is a normal part of Test cricket in the country."Typically, a lot of people say about Test cricket, New Zealand always plays a bit better than it looks. I think the grass coverage and the green tinge sort of makes us wonder what's it going to do? Is it going to nip, bounce or seam? But that's a standard Test wicket," Ravindra said ahead of the opening Test.He also pointed out that the Basin Reserve has produced some good batting performances and exciting matches in recent years."I think the new ball is always going to do that. But you've seen some fantastic scores and great games of cricket played here at the Basin in the last few years. So I expect it to be a good wicket, as it always is."Nice bounce, nice carry. But yeah, it's Test cricket in New Zealand. You're always going to have probably the seamers dominating with a bit of chipping in from the spinners," he added.Ravindra excited about comeback after shoulder injuryRavindra is set to return to action after an eight-week rehabilitation period following a shoulder dislocation.The all-rounder was forced to watch his teammates from the sidelines during his recovery but is now happy to be back in the team."Watching the guys play on TV, you get a little bit of FOMO (Fear Of Missing Out), you want to be out there. I'm super excited, especially in Wellington. It's always nice to have your first game back in three months at your home ground," he said.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Yashasvi Jaiswal's New Zealand Test: Time to switch back on
articles.summary: MUMBAU: For the first time in over a year, Yashasvi Jaiswal heads into a Test series carrying doubts and distractions.
articles.body: MUMBAU: For the first time in over a year, Yashasvi Jaiswal heads into a Test series carrying doubts and distractions.The 24-year-old remains one of India's most gifted young batters, but a stop-start year across formats has left him searching for the consistency that once seemed inevitable. As India prepare for the two-Test series in New Zealand, starting Nov 19 at Wellington's Basin Reserve, the Mumbai left-hander finds himself at a crucial stage of his career.Not long ago, Jaiswal was seen as a three-format certainty. Today, he is effectively a Test specialist. Dropped from India's ODI side despite two hundreds in his last three outings and overlooked for subsequent white-ball assignments in New Zealand, his immediate future rests on Test performances. The New Zealand series, therefore, shapes up as a major test.New Zealand's seam-friendly conditions have often exposed technical flaws in visiting batters, especially openers. Jaiswal, though, arrives with useful preparation. While India's white-ball players moved between formats, he spent time with the India A side, playing three games, scoring two centuries - 102 and 155 - and spending long hours at the crease. Just as importantly, he had an extended red-ball preparation block, a rarity in the modern calendar.Those innings may have helped restore confidence after an indifferent Test tour of Sri Lanka, where he got starts but failed to make a substantial impact and was involved in unnecessary exchanges with opposition bowlers.Former India captain and chief selector Dilip Vengsarkar sympathised with Jaiswal and said the left-hander will have to wait for his chance across formats. Patience, he believes, will be key."Whenever you get an opportunity, you have to perform big and deliver. You can't afford to take any opportunity lightly. Others got opportunities and made the most of them. He has to be patient and, whenever he gets a chance, deliver," Vengsarkar told TOI.The past few months have brought distractions too. Jaiswal's future with Rajasthan Royals has been the subject of speculation, with the opener understood to be keen on moving to a team that sees him as a leader. Those close to him say he remains eager to force his way back into India's ODI and T20I plans.The rise of Vaibhav Suryavanshi, Abhishek Sharma and Sanju Samson in T20Is, along with the consistency of Shubman Gill and Rohit Sharma at the top in ODIs, has pushed him down the pecking order. articles.title: Exclusive Interview | Shubman Gill's hunger and appetite to improve set him apart: Kane Williamson
articles.summary: WELLINGTON: Kane Williamson has been Shubman Gill's go-to man before every important overseas Test assignment.
articles.body: WELLINGTON: Kane Williamson has been Shubman Gill's go-to man before every important overseas Test assignment. The Indian captain reached out to him before the tour of England last year and repeated the drill before arriving in New Zealand. While the English summer involved conversations about technical adjustments, last month's focus in Auckland was on getting acclimatised to the conditions.Gill arrived early with Gurnoor Brar, and Williamson arranged a camp for his former Gujarat Titans teammate before the ODI series got underway. In an exclusive conversation with TOI, Williamson, who has released his autobiography, "The Bare Margins", opens up about his bond with Gill and the two-Test series.Excerpts:You are on Shubman Gill's speed dial before he travels for a Test series. How has discussing batting with him been?Look, he is a lovely human being and a proper student of the game. Our relationship goes back a long way, from our time together at Gujarat Titans, and he keeps reaching out from time to time to discuss batting. We have had numerous conversations about the different nuances of the game, and his appetite to grow and improve as a batter is commendable.Did he reach out before coming to New Zealand too?He arrived early in Auckland and wanted to start preparing well before the long series. So I helped arrange a few days of practice for him to ensure he got some work in before the series started. He constantly wants to improve, so it's no surprise that his career is on an upward curve. As I said, his hunger and appetite to constantly improve set him apart.Gill had a very good series in England. Do you think New Zealand will be the most challenging tour of his career?He had a very good series in England, both he and the team. And I am really excited to see him bat in these conditions. He is a world-class batter, and I am sure he will enjoy batting here. The conditions are challenging for any visiting team, but I am sure he will be up for the task when the series gets underway.There's a lot of chatter about the wind in Wellington from a bowling standpoint. But is the challenge equally stiff for batters?Well, yes (laughs). The crosswinds can sometimes blow you off your stance, so you need to be ready for that. You also need to factor in which way the wind is blowing because if it's against the bowler, deliveries from one end can come slower than from the other. And batters from both teams will face that challenge. But it's about getting used to it quickly and just factoring in the direction. For bowlers, it's going to be a bigger challenge, and I expect Mohammed Siraj from India to do the heavy lifting because he is the kind of character who bowls with a big heart and can bowl long spells.What would your advice be to batters from both teams?Balance is key. If a batter remains nice and balanced, especially when the spell of crosswinds begins, it should be fine. I wouldn't say there is a need for other changes. Just balance and staying nice and steady at the crease are important.Both teams have potent bowling attacks, and we saw a trailer of that in the ODI series. But will this series be more about how well the batters perform?I feel the conditions will be more or less similar across the two venues. There will be nice bounce, carry and movement on offer for the bowlers, but there will be periods when the surfaces ease out. There will be that initial help for the bowlers, as there always has been, but both teams also have enough quality in their batting groups.How did you get the idea to pen your cricket journey into a book, The Bare Margins?Well, I wasn't really keen initially, but my friend convinced me to do it. And it was really exciting to pen down my thoughts honestly, and it felt like a full circle for me. Obviously, I have mentioned my journey, New Zealand's cricket journey, the role of Brendon McCullum and many other things, as honestly as I could.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Must be taught how to behave': Vengsarkar criticises India players' conduct against Pakistan after U19 Asia Cup win
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Former India captain and chief selector Dilip Vengsarkar has criticised the conduct of players following India's victory over Pakistan in the
articles.body: MUMBAI: Former India captain and chief selector Dilip Vengsarkar has criticised the conduct of players following India's victory over Pakistan in the Under-19 Asia Cup final on Saturday, saying such celebrations send the wrong message to young cricketers and undermine the spirit of the game.The scenes that followed India's dramatic triumph sparked intense debate even among the sane and reasonable cricket fans in India after Indian players rushed onto the field and celebrated wildly, with emotions spilling over at the end of the fiercely contested clash. One player got very close to Pakistan's wicket-keeper and screamed obscenities in his face. A few others directed profanities at the Pakistan dressing room and players with indecent gestures.Vengsarkar, who was part of many feisty India-Pakistan battles himself, however, felt there could be no justification for such behaviour, regardless of the occasion. "This is not good for the game at all. Youngsters watch these things on television and then try to emulate them when they play Under-14, Under-16 or Under-19 cricket. Where are we going if this continues? Players must be taught how to behave on and off the field, whether through the National Cricket Academy (COE) or other channels," he told TOI.The former batting great acknowledged the intense emotions associated with India-Pakistan contests. "I understand that India-Pakistan matches are highly emotional and passions run high. But that does not mean you behave in a manner that is unacceptable. Such behaviour creates the wrong impression on youngsters," he said, urging players to maintain decorum.Vengsarkar, who is actively involved in promoting grassroots cricket in Mumbai, revealed that he has increasingly noticed similar behaviour at the junior level. "I see the same thing at my academies. Whenever teams win, players run onto the ground, remove the stumps and start dancing. This never happened before. They watch these scenes on television and then copy them," he said.Demanding stronger intervention from cricket's governing authorities, Vengsarkar says the ICC, Asian Cricket Council and match officials must send a clear message on acceptable conduct. "There has to be some sort of code of conduct. A stronger message must come from the ICC, the ACC and from match referees," he said.The 70-year-old also suggested that players should be formally briefed before tournaments begin. "Before every tournament, officials should address the players, whether they are Under-19, Under-17 or Under-23 cricketers, and clearly explain what is acceptable behaviour and what is not," he said.While acknowledging that match officials may find it difficult to control spontaneous celebrations after a last-ball finish, Vengsarkar said coaches too must play a proactive role. "I saw Bangladesh do something similar a couple of years ago (2020 U-19 WC final), Pakistan did it during this tournament and now India has done it. There cannot be any justification. Nobody should be doing it," he said."The important thing is to set the right example. Young cricketers are always watching and learning from what they see at the highest level."Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
